To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• The customary legal system is the preferred means of dispute resolution for most people, and the only viable option for the vast majority of the poor.
• Customary legal systems are the predominant means of resolving disputes in many parts of the world.

the rule of law practitioners in the field should: 1) recognize the importance of customary law in the lives of most people in the developing and post conflict world; 2) recognize the importance that the rule of the law practitioners can play in the relationship between state and customary law; 3) understand the different ways in which customary and state law systems can be integrated; and 4) be aware of the potential risks and benefits of each of the options.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
how the rule of law can be advanced by supporting both state and customary legal systems, which are complementary, rather than competing, institutions.

how to build a justice system that works for all people, including those who live in rural areas, who have limited access to formal legal services and who are more likely to rely on customary legal institutions for dispute resolution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the best policy is to promote the rule of law through a mix of both state and non state institutions, including customary law institutions, and that this should be the default position of development practitioners.
the best way to support the rule of law is to support the rule by law, and the rule by law requires a balanced approach to both state and customary legal systems.
(1) Customary legal systems are a critical component of the justice system in most developing countries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need to understand and respect customary legal systems, and to find ways to support both state and customary legal institutions to work together in a way that advances the rule of law.

the paper is an attempt to provide guidance to development practitioners on the role of customary law in the justice sector and to suggest how to build complementary customary and state legal institutions in a manner that advances development goals.
we have been able to identify a number of good practices for programs that support customary and state legal institutions in co existing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
customary legal systems, when supported by the right interventions, can be an effective means of dispute resolution, a source of social capital and a means to achieve development goals.
the rule of law cannot be built in a single system.
there is no one right way to engage customary law.
